svg.title: Spatial Logistics of the RAMC Evacuation Chain: CCS Railheads, Canal Barges & Coastal Base Hospitals (1914–1918)
svg.desc: True 1:10m GIS logistics atlas of the British Sector of the Western Front, English Channel, and South-East England (1914–18), mapping the spatial RAMC evacuation chain from frontline Regimental Aid Posts (Menin Road/Ypres and Albert) and Field Ambulance Dressing Stations to forward railhead Casualty Clearing Stations (Lijssenthoek/Remy Siding, Brandhoek, Agny, and Gezaincourt), Red Cross Ambulance Train trunk lines via Hazebrouck, St-Omer, Amiens, and Abbeville, smooth-gliding hospital canal barges on the Yser, Aa, and Somme canals, coastal Base Hospitals at Calais, Wimereux, Boulogne, and Étaples, and cross-Channel hospital ships to Dover, Southampton, and Queen’s Hospital, Sidcup.

text.tspan: Menin Rd / Hellfire Corner → Ypres & Albert

Queen’s Hospital, Sidcup (Harold Gillies Facial Surgery, 1917)

g.text: Frontline RAP → ADS/MDS Motor Ambulance Relay

Hospital Canal Barge Waterways (Yser, Aa & Somme)
Vibration-free transport for severe skull, spine & chest wounds

svg.text: EDEXCEL GCSE HISTORY • PAPER 1 (SECTION A): THE CHAIN OF EVACUATION ON THE WESTERN FRONT (KT5.4)
Spatial Logistics of the RAMC Evacuation Chain: CCS Railheads, Barges & Base Hospitals (1914–18)
Moving urgent surgery forward to railhead CCS hubs (7–10 miles behind the front) beat the 24-hour gas-gangrene window, while ambulance
trains, smooth canal barges, FANY convoys, coastal Base Hospitals, and hospital ships linked trenches to specialist UK care at Sidcup.
